source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles
finding: Full text read this session (the PDF has a text layer once fully downloaded; the earlier truncated copy was unreadable). Definition 2.4: a diagnosis is a subset-minimal set A of components such that SD + OBS + {AB(c): c in A} + {not AB(c): c not in A} is consistent. Theorem 4.4: A is a diagnosis iff A is a minimal hitting set of the collection of conflict sets. Corollary 4.5: the same holds using only the minimal conflict sets.
numbers: Full adder example: two minimal conflict sets give three diagnoses, {X1}, {X2,O1}, {X2,A2}. Proposition 3.2: the empty set is the only diagnosis iff the observation does not conflict with all-components-normal.
quote: A diagnosis for (SD, COMPONENTS, OBS) is a minimal set A
limits: Consistency in first-order logic is undecidable, so the theory is computable only where a consistency test exists. Reiter presents parsimony as a principle (assumption), not a law.
agent_relevance: K01 now rests on the primary text. The empty-conflict case is exactly the no-diagnosis-needed case: if no check fails, the agent should not revise anything.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles
finding: Reiter's own algorithm builds a pruned HS-tree breadth-first, so diagnoses come out in order of increasing cardinality, and he says you may stop at level k if larger diagnoses are highly improbable. If the conflict finder returns only minimal conflict sets, no edge is ever marked redundant, so tree generation is simpler. The theorem prover is a black box that returns one conflict per call and should cache intermediate work.
numbers: Level 1 holds all single-component diagnoses, level 2 all pairs, and so on. Example 4.9 (Davis device, 5 components M1, M2, M3, A1, A2) has two single-fault diagnoses {M1} and {A1} plus multiple-fault ones.
quote: diagnoses are computed in order of increasing cardinality
limits: The cap is justified by belief about improbability, not by any measured loss. The paper reports no timing or size data.
agent_relevance: A size cap is part of the original theory, not a later hack. Gap 3 is about how large k must be, not whether to cap. A conflict finder that returns minimal conflicts removes the Greiner problem.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles
finding: Theorem 5.7: when every current diagnosis predicts either H or not-H and H is then measured, every old diagnosis predicting H survives, every old one predicting not-H is dropped, and any NEW diagnosis is a strict superset of some old diagnosis that predicted not-H. Corollary 5.8: new diagnoses are multiple-fault diagnoses. Corollary 5.9: surviving single-fault diagnoses are exactly the old single faults that predicted H. So divide-and-conquer is valid for single faults, not for all diagnoses.
numbers: Example 5.6/5.10 (Davis device): measuring out(M2)=5 replaced four old diagnoses by four new supersets {M1,M2,M3}, {M1,M2,A2}, {M2,M3,A1}, {M2,A1,A2}. Measuring out(M1)=6 leaves {A1}, {M2,M3}, {M2,A2}.
limits: Theorem is for the logical (non-probabilistic) theory and assumes measurements are reliable.
agent_relevance: After a new observation (a second attempt, a new check result), a size-1 cap can silently lose the true culprit because it has moved to a superset. Rule for S6: recompute, do not filter; when the single-fault set empties, raise the cap by one.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles
finding: Reiter's theory contains no probabilities. Section 7 says de Kleer and Williams (1987) go beyond his theory by computing diagnosis probabilities and using them to pick the next measurement, and that their characterization of diagnoses corresponds to his Theorem 4.4 but lacks a formalization. He credits the conflict-set idea to de Kleer's 1976 LOCAL system. Section 6 links diagnoses to extensions of a default theory.
numbers: Reiter's measurement section is qualitative only (Theorems 5.5 to 5.9), with no entropy or expected-cost criterion.
limits: The de Kleer and Williams paper itself could NOT be opened: the Linkoping mirror now redirects to an HTML 404 page, and Elsevier and ACM returned 403 or an HTML stub. Claims about priors, Bayes updating of candidates and entropy probe choice stay second-hand (a05, a09, a10, a24).
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 6: probability ranking must be sourced to de Kleer and Williams, not Reiter. Whatever the schema says about probability ranking or entropy probe choice is still backed only by secondary sources.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's Hitting-Set Tree for Sequential Diagnosis (preprint), re-read for Greiner, soundness and completeness remarks
finding: Rodler says the flaw Greiner et al. (1989) found in Reiter's pruning does not arise in his algorithm because only minimal conflicts are used as node labels. He still needs a node-replacement step for completeness, citing Greiner. Best-first soundness (only minimal diagnoses returned) needs each component to be more likely nominal than faulty; he enforces it by scaling probabilities by a constant c in (0, 0.5). He notes deciding whether one more minimal diagnosis exists is NP-hard (Bylander et al. 1991), so completeness holds only with unlimited time and memory.
numbers: DynamicHS beat HS-Tree in 96% of sessions, median saving 52%, max 75%, on 20 real knowledge-base diagnosis problems. At least O(|K|) prover calls per conflict (Marques-Silva et al. 2013).
limits: An author's own restatement, not an independent bug hunt. No third-party test of the Greiner correction was found. Pill, Quaritsch and Wotawa 2011 and 2012 could not be fetched (search budget out, no stable URL).
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partly answered: the known fix is minimal conflicts only plus a replacement step; no remaining bugs reported, but no independent test either. Soundness of probability-ordered search needs prior fail rate below 0.5 per step, which a step-failure-rate prior may break on hard problems.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: 3,400 math solutions with a human-marked earliest erroneous step (or all correct). Many solutions with a CORRECT final answer still contain a process error, and the share grows with difficulty. So a final-answer check used as the only consistency test gives an empty conflict on many faulty traces.
numbers: Process errors among correct-final-answer solutions: GSM8K 3.5% (7 of 200), MATH 18.8% (94 of 500), OlympiadBench 32.2% (161 of 500), Omni-MATH 51.8% (259 of 500). Full 3-of-3 annotator agreement: 66.7% down to 47.8% on erroneous items, 95.9% down to 80.1% on correct ones. Mean steps per solution 5.1 to 8.9.
limits: Math word problems only; solutions sampled from open models; earliest-error labels are human judgement and agreement drops on hard items, so labels are noisiest where errors are most common.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: on real traces an answer-level oracle gives empty conflicts for a large share of flawed reasoning. The agent needs step-level checks (recompute, units, constraint tests) or it will wrongly stop at S9.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Step-level blame by prompted general models beat small learned process reward models (PRMs) trained on Monte Carlo step labels, and PRMs fell faster on hard sets. Reasoning models did best. The authors say MC labels are on-policy and corrupted by right-answer-wrong-step cases.
numbers: Average F1 over four subsets: Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B 31.5; Skywork-PRM-1.5B 36.4; Skywork-PRM-7B 42.1; Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K (human labels) 56.5; prompted Llama-3.3-70B 58.0; prompted Qwen2.5-72B 61.2; GPT-4o 61.9 (79.2 GSM8K, 51.4 OlympiadBench); o1-mini 87.9 (93.2 GSM8K, 87.2 OlympiadBench). F1 is the harmonic mean of accuracy on erroneous and on correct samples.
limits: Table 3 text was scrambled in extraction; the QwQ-32B-Preview row was not read cleanly, so it is not quoted. Models are 2024 vintage.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a cheap learned prior (a PRM) did NOT beat a prompted critic. No evidence yet that a cheap prior such as past step failure rate beats model-stated confidence; the only direct evidence on learned scorers points the other way.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2025, TMLR) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 as its own verifier in a generate, critique, re-prompt loop does worse than a single answer, because the verifier rejects many correct answers. With a sound external verifier the same loop gives large gains. This answers gap 8 for the same-model-as-oracle case, for verification, though not for QXR-style pruning.
numbers: 100 instances per domain. Accuracy single prompt / LLM+LLM / LLM+sound verifier with binary feedback: Game of 24 5/3/36; Graph Coloring 16/2/38; Blocksworld 40/55/60; Mystery Blocksworld 4/0/10. LLM verifier false negative rate: Game of 24 20.7% (213/1029), Blocksworld 15.48% (24/155), Mystery Blocksworld 97.09% (100/103), Graph Coloring 95.8% (113/118 as extracted). False positive rate 10.4% (320/3071) on Game of 24, 6.5% (25/382) on Blocksworld.
limits: GPT-4 (2023-24) only; four formal toy-like domains; 15 backprompts max; chain-of-thought verification raised Game of 24 verification accuracy from 87% to 99% but more than doubled output tokens. Newer reasoning models not tested. Table 2 text was scrambled in extraction, so some cells are uncertain.
agent_relevance: A noisy LLM oracle collapses an iterative repair loop. Conflict generation must come from code or a sound checker. Re-test with a reasoning-model verifier before assuming the 2024 result holds today.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2025, TMLR) On the Self-Verification Limitations of Large Language Models on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: With a sound verifier, the detail of the critique mattered in one domain only, and plain repeated sampling matched the critique loops. This is the closest existing equal-budget comparison to the schema's core bet, and it favours best-of-N.
numbers: Accuracy (single prompt / binary feedback / first-error feedback / all-error feedback / sampling k=15 / k=25 / self-consistency k=15): Game of 24 5/36/38/NA/28/42/6; Graph Coloring 16/38/37/34/40/44/14; Blocksworld 40/60/87/83/68/72/42; Mystery Blocksworld 4/10/8/6/9/14/4. First-error feedback beat binary feedback by 27 points only on Blocksworld; sampling at k=25 matched or beat the feedback loops on 3 of 4 domains.
limits: Loops allow up to 15 backprompts; tokens per round differ from tokens per sample, so equal compute is approximate. Feedback names one error, not a minimal conflict over several attempts. GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 4: no support yet for conflict feedback beating plain sampling. Treat best-of-N with a sound checker as the baseline to beat, and run the comparison on current models.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Sequential revision and parallel sampling are complementary, and the best split depends on difficulty and budget. A revision model that sees its previous answers turns many correct answers into wrong ones unless a selector picks the best in the chain. Compute-optimal allocation beats plain best-of-N.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* finetuned for revision, MATH. About 38% of correct answers were converted to incorrect by naive revision. Easy questions favour purely sequential revision; hard ones a mix. Compute-optimal strategy matches best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute. Revision pass@1 keeps improving beyond the 4 revision steps it was trained for.
limits: Capability-specific finetuning for revision was required; one model family and one benchmark; difficulty is estimated with a verifier. Revision here has no localization step, so it does not test a diagnosis-guided edit.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: any revise-the-culprit loop needs a keep-the-best rule (S9) or it destroys good answers (about 38% here). It also gives a design for the equal-token test: sweep the sequential-to-parallel split per difficulty.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) keeps rising with samples over four orders of magnitude, but selection without a real checker stalls. Where an automatic verifier exists, sampling turns coverage into accuracy.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples (single-sample state of the art 43%). MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, while majority vote or reward-model selection moved only 40.50% to 41.41%. Gemma-2B CodeContests coverage up over 300x from 0.02%.
limits: Coverage equals pass@k with an oracle; verifier-based gains depend on the checker being exact (unit tests, proof checker).
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the equal-token baseline is strong exactly when a code checker exists. Diagnosis-guided revision must beat many cheap samples, and can only win when checks are partial or samples are costly. Supports G3 (code checks, not model judgment).

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Counterfactual edits of a chain of thought (truncate it, insert a mistake into one sentence and resample the rest, paraphrase, filler tokens) show that final answers depend on the stated steps very unevenly across tasks, and that larger models depend on them less. So revise step i and re-run tests step i only where the chain is causally used.
numbers: Area over the curve, early answering / adding mistakes, 175B model: AQuA 0.44/0.52, LogiQA 0.26/0.31, MMLU 0.12/0.21, HellaSwag 0.12/0.23, TruthfulQA 0.11/0.20, OpenBookQA 0.07/0.15, ARC-Challenge 0.05/0.11, ARC-Easy 0.02/0.07 (higher means the answer depends more on the CoT). Inserted mistakes judged plausible at least 80% of the time. Faithfulness gets worse from 13B to 175B on most tasks.
limits: Anthropic internal 2022-era models, multiple-choice tasks, mistakes written by a pretrained model. Current reasoning models not tested. Table 2 row order was read from the text layout and matches the paper's statement that AQuA and LogiQA are most faithful.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: counterfactual step edits transfer as a method, but their value runs from near zero to substantial by task. Check causal dependence on a dev set before trusting remove-the-suspect-and-see-if-it-recovers on text steps.

source: Bogdan, Macar, Nanda, Conmy (2025) Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
finding: Sentence-level counterfactual resampling on reasoning traces: for each sentence, 100 rollouts with it and 100 with a resampled replacement; importance is the KL divergence of the final-answer distributions. Planning and uncertainty-management sentences carry the highest counterfactual importance. Read through a fetch summary of the first 100,000 of 124,053 characters (the PDF download failed), so numbers are as reported by that tool.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B on MATH, 20 problems with 25 to 75% solve rate, one correct and one incorrect trace each, 40 responses. Mean 144.2 sentences (95% CI 116.7 to 171.8) and 4,208 tokens per response. That is about 14,400 rollouts per trace, on the order of 10^7 generated tokens if rollouts are full length. Category shares: active computation 32.7%, fact retrieval 20.1%, plan generation 15.5%, uncertainty management 14.0%. With 100 resamples, the 95% CI is at worst about +-10% on answer accuracy.
limits: Authors call it preliminary; 20 problems; one model family; overdetermined sentences and error correction not handled; adaptive resampling left to future work. Full text not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: counterfactual re-runs on prose steps are far too costly for a per-item loop (G11) at 100 rollouts per sentence. Use coarse steps (about 5 to 10), few rollouts, or checks that run in code. Planning and uncertainty steps matter most, which hints at which steps to treat as components.

source: Karimi Bavandpour and Bercher (2026) LLM-Only PDDL Domain Repair with Open-Weight Models
finding: Re-read for the effort question. The authors do NOT establish why high effort hurts some models. They suggest that reasoning jointly over many long plans is combinatorial and may exceed the context window, and point to their Table 4, which contains context-limit errors and unparsable outputs. They list isolating prompt length, explicit reasoning requests and examples as future work. The prompt here is shorter and has no reasoning request or one-shot example, which lowered GPT-4o.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B no traces: default F1 .53 / test rate .50, high effort .37 / .40. With traces: default .49 / .57, high effort .15 / .09. GPT-OSS-20B with traces: F1 .23 to .41 (test rate .26 to .55). GLM 5.2 no traces .85 to .87; Mistral Small 4 .13 to .41. GPT-4o .46 (earlier prompt) vs .38 (short prompt).
limits: Cause untested: context overflow, parse failures and over-long reasoning are confounded. Single suite, open-weight models, public benchmark so recall is possible.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Failures with traces may be partly mechanical (context-limit and parse errors counted as misses). Set per-model caps (G11) from a dev-set effort curve that logs parse and overflow failures apart from wrong answers.

source: Gema et al. (2025, TMLR) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
finding: Longer reasoning lowers accuracy on some tasks, through different mechanisms per model. This is direct evidence that distraction and framing overfit can cause more-reasoning-hurts. Few-shot examples largely cured the regression-task failure, so prompt format matters.
numbers: Claude Opus 4 on counting with distractors: accuracy falls from nearly 100% to about 85 to 90% as reasoning lengthens. DeepSeek R1, natural overthinking, five distractors: 70% falls to 30%. o-series resists distractors but overfits to familiar framings. All tested models degrade on Zebra-puzzle deduction as reasoning grows. Trend labels need over 2% accuracy change with non-overlapping 95% CIs.
limits: Synthetic tasks built to elicit the effect; not repair tasks. Models: Claude Sonnet 3.7 and 4, Opus 4, o3-mini, o3, o4-mini, Qwen3 32B, QwQ 32B, DeepSeek R1. The PDDL repair setting was not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: supports overthinking and distraction as one mechanism. Fit G11 caps per model and task type, and filter irrelevant evidence (long traces, unrelated failures) before the model sees it.

source: Own Monte Carlo simulation run this session (not literature). Script: scratchpad/sim/sim.py
finding: Toy model of conflicts on a 20-step trace: k hidden faulty steps; m checks, each covering a chain of up to 6 consecutive steps ending at a random step; a check fails if its support holds a fault (miss rate fn) or by false alarm (fp). Conflicts are the minimal failed supports; minimal hitting sets are computed exactly up to size cap. When the number of true errors exceeds the cap, a diagnosis within the cap often does not exist, which is detectable. A cap of k or k+1 finds a true-fault step in nearly all noise-free cases.
numbers: 3,000 trials per cell, n=20, m=8, noise-free. Share of trials with a hitting set of size <= cap: k=1 .73 for any cap; k=2 cap1 .53, cap2 .93; k=3 cap1 .29, cap2 .84, cap3 .98; k=4 cap1 .16, cap2 .67, cap3 .97. Candidate steps (union of diagnoses) at k=3: 0.8 (cap1), 4.7 (cap2), 7.3 (cap3) of 20. With fn=.2 and fp=.05, k=3, cap 3: a true-fault step is in the candidate set in .97 of trials with a non-empty conflict.
limits: Assumes independent, uniformly random faults and checks with known supports; real traces have cascading errors, unknown dependencies and correlated checks. Shape only. NOT evidence about LLM behaviour.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a cap of 2 is enough only if there are at most 2 errors; a cap of 3 covers k up to 4 in about 96% of toy cases while shrinking the search to about 7 of 20 steps. Use no hitting set within cap as the trigger to raise the cap.

source: Own Monte Carlo simulation run this session (not literature). Script: scratchpad/sim/sim.py
finding: Same simulator, other outputs. The share of empty conflicts (faults exist but no check fails) is set by check coverage. Size-1 conflicts get common once errors are multiple. The top-1 step chosen by hitting sets is only modestly better than simple blame rules.
numbers: Empty conflict (m=8 checks, noise-free): .27 at k=1, .07 at k=2, .02 at k=3. With m=16 and fn=.2: .06 (k=1), .003 (k=3). Size-1 conflicts with m=8: .08 (k=1) rising to .28 (k=4); .25 to .41 with m=16. Top-1 pick is a true fault (noise-free): hitting-set pick, cap 1, .44/.48/.49/.51 for k=1..4; cap 2 .44/.52/.57/.60; random step from the union of conflicts .33 to .37; blame the last step of the smallest failed check .38/.45/.54/.63; random step of the trace .05 to .21. With fn=.4, fp=.1 the hitting-set pick drops to .21 to .44.
limits: Blame-last-of-smallest-check is strong in the toy because checks are chains ending at the failing step; this favours that rule. The hitting-set advantage over it ranged from +6 points (k=1) to about -3 (k=4, cap 2 .60 vs .63).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: do not expect hitting sets to beat a good local blame rule by much on single-error traces; the gain should appear with multiple errors and overlapping checks. Count empty and size-1 conflicts on a real dev set first. If most are empty, add checks before adding diagnosis machinery.
